summary.headline: Very safe and steadily growing, but its spare capital holds returns below what investors need
summary.text: Central Finance (CFIN.N0000) is one of Sri Lanka's oldest and most conservatively run finance companies (vehicle leasing and loans), and also owns 19.7% of Nations Trust Bank and most of Central Industries. It is very safe: core capital 31.9% against a 10% minimum, equity about half of total assets, gross non-performing loans 1.8%, and group profit every year for over a decade, growing EPS from Rs 30.80 (2021/22) to Rs 45.09 (2025/26) and Rs 28.73 in the six months to September 2026. At Rs 231.50 (CSE, 11 November 2026) it trades at only 0.59x its group NAV of Rs 395.47 and 4.7x trailing earnings, which looks cheap. But because it holds so much capital, its return on equity is only 12–14%, below the 18% I require, so it deserves to trade below book. Three methods put fair value at about Rs 219, so the price is about 6% above it: close to fair. I'd buy at up to Rs 186.40 (the share was Rs 190.25 at its 12-month low) and treat under Rs 164.40 as a strong buy. Watch the company's own profit, which fell 14% in the half year as interest costs rose 76% on fast loan growth; the group was carried by Nations Trust Bank.

quality.reason: Exceptionally well capitalised, profitable every year and paying every year; the weakness is a 12–14% return on equity.

tests.label: Return on equity of 15% or more
tests.note: Group 12–14% every year since 2021/22; company 10.5% in 2025/26. Low because equity is about half of assets.

tests.label: Capital comfortably above the minimum (finance company)
tests.note: Minimum 10%; total capital 30.7% (minimum 14%). Down from 47% a year earlier as loans grew.

tests.label: Steady profit: no loss in five years, no one-offs
tests.note: Group EPS rose every year from 2021/22 to 2025/26; impairment reversals help but are small (Rs 0.25bn of Rs 9.7bn operating profit in the half year).

tests.label: Profit turns into cash and dividends
tests.note: Dividends paid every year; payout is low (about 14% of group profit), with the rest compounding book value about 11% a year.

valuation.note: Fair value weights the bear/base/bull averages of three methods 30/50/20 (about 0.55x group NAV). The dividend model isn't used because the payout is very low; see the method readings.

highlights.title: Six months to September 2026 (unaudited)
highlights.text: Group profit to shareholders up 17% to Rs 6.53bn (EPS Rs 28.73 against Rs 24.50), helped by a 44% rise in its share of Nations Trust Bank's profit (Rs 3.33bn). The company itself earned Rs 2.86bn, down 14%: interest expenses rose 76% as borrowings funded loan growth, and impairment reversals shrank to Rs 0.26bn from Rs 0.90bn.

highlights.title: Rapid loan growth
highlights.text: Loans, leases and hire purchase rose 58% in 2025/26 to Rs 104.8bn and another 13% to Rs 118.9bn by September 2026, funded by borrowings (up to Rs 29.9bn from Rs 20.7bn in six months) as well as deposits (Rs 51.2bn). Core capital fell from 47% to 32%, still far above the minimum.

highlights.title: 2025/26 (audited)
highlights.text: Group profit to shareholders Rs 10.25bn (Rs 9.92bn), EPS Rs 45.09; company profit Rs 6.04bn, ROE 10.5%. Gross non-performing loans fell to 1.65% from 2.76%. Dividend Rs 6.50 (unchanged).

highlights.title: Nations Trust Bank stake must be cut
highlights.text: The group owns 19.7% of Nations Trust Bank's voting shares, worth about Rs 18.8bn at Rs 330.75 (Rs 82.80 per CF share) against a book value of Rs 23.4bn. Banking rules require the group to reduce its voting stake to 15%.

methodReadings.reading: Group NAV at 30 September 2026; 0.59x. NAV has compounded about 11% a year since 2021/22.
Group 12–14% for five years; company 10.5%. Below the 18% I require, so a discount to book is justified.
On trailing group EPS of Rs 49.32. Ten-year range of year-end P/E (company EPS) 2.9–8.6x, average about 5.2x.
Rs 6.50 a year, about 14% of group profit. A dividend model gives only about Rs 60 because so little is paid out, so it isn't used in fair value.
Three times the 10% minimum: room to grow loans without raising capital.
The Nations Trust Bank stake alone is worth Rs 82.80 a share at market; the finance company's own book value is Rs 271 a share.

models.name: Justified price to book
models.comment: Book value Rs 395.47 × (ROE − growth) ÷ (cost of equity − growth): ROE 11% / 12.5% / 14%.

models.name: Residual income
models.comment: ROE moving from 13% to 11% / 12.5% / 14% over ten years; 15% payout.

modelsNote: A finance company, so instead of a cash-flow DCF I used residual income and a justified price-to-book, alongside P/E. The dividend model is left out because Central Finance pays out only about 14% of group profit.

scenarios.common: 10-year government bond about 12.4% (9 Nov 2026) plus about 5.5 points for a leveraged lender. Base 2026/27 EPS assumes the second half is about 10% above last year's (Rs 20.59).

sensitivity.title: Residual income base case, Rs per share
sensitivity.note: Today's Rs 231.50 needs a long-run ROE of about 13.5% at an 18% cost of equity.

buyPlan.note: About Rs 96,480 in total, against Rs 115,750 at Rs 231.50.
buyPlan.realism: Rs 186.40 is just below the 12-month low of Rs 190.25 and about 19% below today's price, so it's realistic in a market dip.

higher: ROE rising above 15% as the extra capital is put to work in loans.
Selling the excess Nations Trust Bank shares at or above book value and returning cash.
lower: Bad loans rising from the fast loan growth (vehicle loans in a downturn).
Margins squeezed further by higher borrowing costs.
A forced sale of Nations Trust Bank shares below book value.

notes.disclaimer: These are estimates from the annual reports to March 2026 and the interim reports to September 2026 (unaudited). This is analysis, not personal financial advice.

Decision box.Verdict: About fair: 6% above fair value of Rs 219.
Decision box.Expected yearly return at Rs 231.50: About 11% a year: dividend 2.8% + book growth about 10% − about 2% a year if the price moved to fair value.
Decision box.Confidence: Medium to high: a predictable, conservatively run business; the main uncertainty is the fast loan growth.
Decision box.Margin of safety: Buy 15% below fair value (Rs 186.40), strong buy 25% below (Rs 164.40).

Business and moat.What it does: Vehicle leasing, hire purchase and loans (about 80% of lending is leases), deposits, plus a 19.7% stake in Nations Trust Bank, Central Industries (PVC pipes) and vehicle and tyre trading. 110 branches.
Business and moat.Moat: Moderate: nearly 70 years in vehicle finance, a strong brand, low funding costs from a large deposit base, and very strong capital.
Business and moat.Growth: Loans grew 58% in 2025/26 and 13% in the six months to September 2026 as vehicle imports resumed.

Management and governance.Ownership: Corporate Services (Pvt) Ltd 16.1%, E.H. Wijenaike (director) 15.4%, EPF 10.0%, Thurston Investments 5.8%, Hallsville Frontier 5.8%.
Management and governance.Record: Conservative: profitable through the 2022 crisis, NPLs kept low, dividends every year.

Sri Lanka checks.Interest rates: Watch: borrowing costs rose 76% in the half year; margins depend on rates.
Sri Lanka checks.Vehicle market: Watch: vehicle import rules and taxes drive leasing demand.
Sri Lanka checks.Bank regulation: The Nations Trust Bank stake must fall to 15% of voting shares.

Investment case and sell rules.Why own it: A very safe, steadily compounding lender near book-discount levels, with a valuable bank stake.
Investment case and sell rules.Sell triggers: Price more than 30% above fair value (above Rs 285); NPLs rising above 4%; or capital falling below 20%.

Key ratios (five-year trend).Loans, leases and HP: Mar 2024 Rs 50.2bn · Mar 2025 Rs 66.1bn · Mar 2026 Rs 104.8bn · Sep 2026 Rs 118.9bn

What this analysis doesn't cover: Nations Trust Bank's own reports (only its market price and CF's share of profit were used).

Cost of equity 19.5% / 18% / 16.5%; long-run ROE 11% / 12.5% / 14%; growth 5% / 6% / 7%; 2026/27 EPS Rs 48 / 52 / 54 at 4.5 / 5.5 / 6.5 times.
